forces: Contralto and tenor soloists, mixed chorus, organ and orchestra
performers: Oralia Domínguez, contralto; Raymond Amade, tenor; J. J. Grunenwald, organ; Chorale Élisabeth Brasseur; Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
intro: In Boulanger’s setting of Psalm 130, dedicated to her father’s memory, tuba and solo cello share a low line. Igor Markevitch conducts, and the contralto Oralia Domínguez sings the long solo at the centre of the work.

sections.label: Intro · Tuba and solo cello
sections.mNote: A descending phrase above low organ and plucked strings.

sections.label: A · Choir in octaves
sections.mNote: Quiet repeated notes over a held organ bass.

sections.label: B · Contralto with solo cello
sections.mNote: Clarinet figures climb beneath the solo voice.

sections.label: C · Bassoon, flute and solo strings
sections.mNote: A bassoon begins the interlude over running harp notes.

sections.label: D · Contralto and tenor in canon
sections.mNote: The tenor repeats the contralto’s phrase a fifth lower.

sections.label: E · Allegro, low voices and fast strings
sections.mNote: Allegro: detached figures in the wind and strings.

sections.label: Coda · Slow prayer theme, choir, brass, organ
sections.mNote: Brass and organ support the choir’s broad phrases.

cues.title: Opening, tuba and solo cello
cues.text: The organ holds low notes above a soft bass-drum roll and plucked strings. A tuba and a solo cello enter together and fall by a tone. Their line lies deep below the choir, which is silent, and muted horns join it.
cues.evidence: Durand full score (1925), plate D. & F. 10543, p. 1: Lent librement, organ, bass drum, pizzicato cellos and basses; tuba and solo cello from bar 3, muted horns later on the page. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP393069-PMLP430943-N0856389_PDF_1_-1DM.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: B♭ minor in Lili Boulanger’s music
cues.text: Christopher Palmer described B♭ minor as, for Lili, “the key of the abyss, of mourning and despair”. She used it for this psalm and for her Musset setting Pour les funérailles d’un soldat. Gerald Larner noted that modal inflections make the harmonies of the introduction more oppressive still.
cues.evidence: Christopher Palmer, notes for Hyperion CDA66726 (1994): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66726. Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Prelude, violins in the high register
cues.text: The prelude rises to the violins’ high register. First and second violins move upwards through sharps and naturals and briefly play alone. A Poco accel. takes their runs over the top, and the descent broadens at Élargi.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 3–4, after figure 1: high first and second violins, Rubato, Poco accel. and Élargi.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rome and Gargenville, 1914–1917
cues.text: Boulanger began the psalm in Rome in 1914 and completed its orchestration at Gargenville, the family home, in 1917. The last page of the Durand full score is dated Rome–Gargenville 1914–1917.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 90, dated Rome–Gargenville 1914–1917. Helen Julia Minors’s preface (2011) identifies Gargenville as the family home and dates the completed orchestration to 1917. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1001.html

cues.title: Choral entry in octaves
cues.text: The choir enters pp, all four parts singing the same narrow line in octaves. Boulanger marks it sobre, mais intense (restrained, but intense). Bassoons and cellos climb underneath, and the organ holds the bass.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, p. 11, figure 4: Tempo lent, pp sobre, mais intense, octave choral entry, rising bassoons and cellos, sustained organ pedal.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First choral entry
cues.text: Gerald Larner wrote that on its first entry the chorus “merely chants the words”. The vocal line becomes melodic gradually, through a lyrical expansion on the holy names “Iahvé” and “Adonaï”, and moves into sustained supplication.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Dedication to Ernest Boulanger
cues.text: Above the title Boulanger wrote “à la mémoire de mon cher Papa” (to the memory of my dear Papa). Ernest Boulanger died in 1900, when she was six. The dedication stands over the psalm’s first low instrumental notes.
cues.evidence: Lili Boulanger’s dedication on the first page of Psalm 130, completed in 1917, Durand full score (1925), p. 1. Ernest Boulanger’s death and Lili’s age are given in Helen Julia Minors’s preface (2011). https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/1001.html

cues.title: Christopher Palmer and the Markevich recording
cues.text: Christopher Palmer, then a student, first heard Lili Boulanger on “the classic Markevich record originally issued on the Everest label”, this recording. He wrote to Nadia at once and later said the music “effectively changed my life”. In the summer of 1967 he studied with her at Fontainebleau.
cues.evidence: Christopher Palmer, notes for Hyperion CDA66726 (1994): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66726

cues.title: Climax on “Adonaï”; alto solo
cues.text: The quicker second section opens like the first, with soft chanting, and builds to a broad climax on the “Adonaï” material. The chorus then stops and the alto soloist enters with a new melody in E♭ minor, at a slower tempo and in a thinner texture.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Contralto entry with solo cello
cues.text: The choir stops and Oralia Domínguez begins the question about human sin. A solo cello joins her line. Clarinets repeat their rising figures and harps mark the pulse, while divided violins hold very soft chords above the voice.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 37–40, figure 12: contralto entry, solo cello, repeated clarinet and bass-clarinet figures, two harps and divided violins marked ppp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Comité Franco-Américain du Conservatoire
cues.text: When war broke out Lili was at the Villa Medici in Rome. She wrote to fellow musicians to build a support network for those serving in the war, and with Nadia founded the Comité Franco-Américain du Conservatoire. Nadia won the backing of American artists and diplomats.
cues.evidence: Library of Congress, “Lili Boulanger”, Women in French history research guide: https://guides.loc.gov/feminism-french-women-history/famous/lili-boulanger

cues.title: Chorus, “Qui donc pourra tenir?”
cues.text: The chorus repeats “Qui donc pourra tenir?” (who can stand?) with growing insistency. Gerald Larner wrote that the most emphatic statement comes on a fortissimo augmentation of the trumpet call from the introduction.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Interlude, solo bassoon
cues.text: A solo bassoon begins the interlude, marked chanté, calme. Flute, viola and cello follow in turn above semiquavers in the harps and organ. The string sections play muted, while the solo viola and cello play without mutes.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 54–56, Modéré and Rubato interlude: solo bassoon and flute, solo viola and cello, harp and organ semiquavers, selective string-muting instructions.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third section, alto entry
cues.text: Gerald Larner called the third section the turning point of the work. The tempo slows. Over rippling arpeggios in harp and organ, a new woodwind melody passes to the alto, who sings “Mais la clémence est en toi”.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130, third section; the English of the sung line is our translation. https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Igor Markevitch, conductor
cues.text: Igor Markevitch was born in Kiev in 1912. At thirteen he went to Paris to study piano with Alfred Cortot, and in his teens he also studied with Nadia Boulanger and Paul Dukas. At seventeen he composed a work for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes.
cues.evidence: Everest LPBR 6059 (1960), sleeve note on the conductor: https://archive.org/download/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d_djvu.txt

cues.title: Canon for contralto and tenor
cues.text: Domínguez sings a new phrase very softly, and Raymond Amade’s tenor repeats it a fifth lower. Their lines overlap above rising flute figures and falling organ notes. The marking is Sans lenteur — without dragging.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 70–73, figure 19: Sans lenteur, contralto and tenor canon with flute, harp and organ. The fifth-below imitation is also described in Helen Julia Minors’s preface (2011).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fourth section, alto and tenor
cues.text: In the fourth section a tenor joins the alto. Gerald Larner wrote that here Lili’s vision “at last” glimpses “the radiance of major harmonies”, after the modal inflections of the earlier sections.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

cues.title: Performances after her death
cues.text: Lili never heard her finest scores played. Christopher Palmer lists Du fond de l’abîme among those unperformed in her lifetime and adds that when they were performed, “no changes were needed apart from a few modifications of dynamics”.
cues.evidence: Christopher Palmer, notes for Hyperion CDA66726 (1994): https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA66726

cues.title: Allegro, tenors and basses
cues.text: An Allegro follows the choir’s held chords. Tenors and basses begin the promise of redemption while clarinets, bassoons and lower strings play detached figures. The upper strings remove their mutes, more of the orchestra joins, and the tempo increases.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 81–85, figure 22 onwards: Allegro, lower-voice entry, detached wind and string figures, removal of violin mutes and acceleration.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return to Lent, figure 23
cues.text: At figure 23 the tempo changes to Lent. Choir, brass and organ return to broad phrases on God’s name, with the bass moving to a low register beneath them. Instruments drop out one by one in the closing prayer, and after the choir’s release the orchestra plays a final swell.
cues.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 86–90, figure 23 Lent, broad choral phrases and low bass writing; De plus en plus lent and Molto rit. on the final page, with the last instrumental swell after the choir’s release.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Everest LP, side one, 1960
cues.text: Everest put the whole twenty-four-minute psalm on side one of LPBR 6059. The four shorter works filled side two.
cues.evidence: Track listing of the Everest LP, 1960: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d

cues.title: Final climax and ending
cues.text: The work reaches a last climax on “Iahvé, Adonaï”, followed by an expression of hope. Gerald Larner wrote that it ends “without the unambiguous consolation Lili was too honest to provide”.
cues.evidence: Gerald Larner, programme note on Psaume 130: https://geraldlarner.com/work/boulanger-psaume-130

transitions.title: Prelude to the choral entry at figure 4
transitions.how: The B♭ minor prelude slows, and the trombones are marked morendo. At figure 4, Tempo lent, the choir enters on repeated notes in octaves. The organ holds a bass note under the voices while bassoons and cellos rise together. The bass drum plays a soft roll under the first words.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 10–12, figure 4: Rit., morendo trombones, Tempo lent, quiet choir, organ pedal and rising bassoon/cello line.

transitions.title: Contralto and solo cello at figure 12
transitions.how: At figure 12 the chorus holds its final vowel and the metre changes to 3/2. The contralto enters over a solo cello, repeated clarinet figures and harp chords. Divided violins hold ppp above her. The organ plays low notes on the slow pulse, and the brass stop.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 36–38, figure 12: change to 3/2, contralto and solo cello, rising clarinets, harps, organ bass and divided ppp violins.

transitions.title: Solo bassoon at Modéré
transitions.to: C · Bassoon, flute and solo strings
transitions.how: At Modéré the choir releases its last syllable and the brass chords stop. A solo bassoon enters above the organ’s held bass and running notes in the harp. Flute and solo viola follow. The remaining strings put on mutes, and the accompaniment thins.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 53–56: Modéré, choral release, solo bassoon and flute, harps, organ and string-muting instructions.

transitions.title: Solo entries over flute semiquavers
transitions.from: C · Bassoon, flute and solo strings
transitions.to: D · Contralto and tenor in canon
transitions.how: The choir holds its last chord into the new 3/4 metre. At Sans lenteur, the flutes rise in semiquavers and the organ’s right hand descends over a held pedal. The contralto enters very softly. One bar later the tenor enters and repeats her phrase a fifth lower.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 69–73, figure 19: 3/4, Sans lenteur, overlapping choral release and solo entries, flute and organ semiquavers.

transitions.title: Held chord, then runs
transitions.from: D · Contralto and tenor in canon
transitions.to: E · Allegro, low voices and fast strings
transitions.how: The choir’s long chord drops to pp subito before figure 22. At Allegro, bass clarinet and bassoon begin detached runs, and violas and cellos join them. Tenors and basses enter with the new words over accented horn notes. The violins remove their mutes as the short figures move up through the strings.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 81–85, figure 22: pp subito before Allegro, detached lower winds and strings, lower-voice entry, horns and removal of violin mutes.

transitions.title: Allegro to Lent at figure 23
transitions.from: E · Allegro, low voices and fast strings
transitions.to: Coda · Slow prayer theme, choir, brass, organ
transitions.how: Wind and string runs climb to the end of the Allegro. At figure 23 they stop, and the tempo changes to Lent with broad choral phrases. Brass and organ hold the harmony while the double basses play rapid low figures between held notes. The last pages slow further, marked De plus en plus lent and Molto rit., and return to the low instruments of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Durand full score, pp. 85–90: ascending runs, figure 23 Lent, sustained brass and organ, rapid double-bass figures, then De plus en plus lent and Molto rit.

source.title: Lili Boulanger, Psaume CXXX, Durand full score (1925), plate D. & F. 10543
source.locator: Printed pp. 1–4, 11–16, 37–40, 54–58, 66–74, 81–90. The score has contralto and tenor soloists, mixed choir, two harps, organ and a large orchestra including sarrusophone.

timeline.note: Low organ notes sound above a bass-drum roll and plucked cellos and double basses.
Tuba and solo cello descend together. Muted horns join their low line.
After the low wind solos, the first and second violins play high, winding phrases.
The choir enters quietly in octaves. Bassoons and cellos rise beneath it over a held organ bass.
Wind runs climb above the choir while brass and low strings hold the bass.
The contralto sings and the solo cello plays over repeated clarinet figures, harp chords and very soft divided violins.
Bassoon, flute, solo viola and solo cello take turns above running notes in harps and organ.
The contralto returns softly with celesta, harp and organ figures, held violin chords and plucked violas.
The choir takes up the contralto’s prayer, joined by brass and the full string sections.
Contralto and tenor sing in canon above rising flute figures and descending organ notes.
Small groups of singers join the solo voices, overlapping above flute, harp and organ.
Detached clarinet, bassoon and string figures accompany the tenors and basses in the Allegro.
At Lent, broad choral phrases return over brass and organ chords. Double basses play rapid low figures.
The voices sing their last phrase. After the choir stops, organ, low winds, brass and strings play one final swell.

composer.epithet: Composer who won the Prix de Rome at nineteen and, before her death at twenty-four, wrote songs of lost love and settings of psalms.
facts: Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger’s younger daughter; Nadia’s sister
Paul Vidal for composition; Georges Caussade for counterpoint; Nadia at home
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome in composition, 1913
Songs, psalms, chamber and orchestral music; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
In May 1913 five young composers were shut away at the Château de Compiègne, writing a cantata about Faust and Helen of Troy. Someone had sent them champagne. Their joint letter of thanks to the composer Fernand Halphen, dated 31 May and written out by Claude Delvincourt, called them “your young colleagues imprisoned in the château to sing the loves of Faust and Helen”. Lili Boulanger was one of the signatories. She was nineteen, and this was her second attempt at the Prix de Rome, because illness had forced her to withdraw the previous year.

In July she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix for musical composition. Thirty-one of the thirty-six voters of the Académie des Beaux-Arts supported her. Faust et Hélène is scored for a tenor Faust in love with a woman summoned from antiquity, a mezzo-soprano Helen and a baritone devil, with a substantial orchestra. The compulsory text was Eugène Adenis’s adaptation of Goethe. Lili dedicated the score to Nadia, who had won a second prize in 1908.
